regularity: Subordination is the modal settlement when a profession's work is contested
source: Abbott (1988); the programme's census of 470 regulatory bodies: 80 subordination rows against 9 exclusions
laboratory_counterpart: governance of buffer and core work under the status quo
verdict: consistent in rank order; constructs differ
evidence_class: pre-AI institutional allocation (status quo, no tool)
construct: DIFFERENT: written subordination rules of regulatory bodies against the share of synthetic work packets settled
unit_contrast: source: rule rows per body; laboratory: packets in buffer and core rings
failure_criterion: gate or poach share above settle share in contested rings

regularity: Sign-off tasks show far less AI use than their exposure predicts
source: the programme: 53 to 73% less use on two platforms (s547)
laboratory_counterpart: share of precedent cases whose final answer came from the program, against all cases
verdict: consistent in sign by construction; the magnitude is typed
evidence_class: AI-era consistency (follows from the typed tier)
construct: DIFFERENT: reserved sign-off tasks in platform usage data against Tier 3 knowledge cases
unit_contrast: source: task usage within occupation; laboratory: packets by tier
failure_criterion: not falsifiable in this design (Tier 3 cases are never compiled by construction)

regularity: Licensed occupations adopt generative AI less than their exposure predicts
source: the programme (s631): -0.25 to -0.29 SD per SD of licensing on two releases; README Table 4b
laboratory_counterpart: share of work in which the program is involved, licensed against unlicensed occupations
verdict: consistent in sign; not attributable to the gate
note: the project's own counterfactual (CF1, no sign-off penalty) leaves within-occupation uptake unchanged, so the contrast comes from the typed content of licensed occupations' work, not from the gate penalty
construct: related: adoption net of exposure against program involvement by occupation
unit_contrast: source: occupations, SD of licensing; laboratory: 18 occupations, gate dummy
failure_criterion: licensed involvement at or above unlicensed involvement

regularity: Relaxing a sign-off requirement lowers prices without lowering quality where the work's errors are observable
source: Kleiner, Marier, Park, and Wing (2016), nurse-practitioner scope of practice: prices of a routine medical exam are 3 to 16% HIGHER where rules are more restrictive (not a 3 to 16% fall from the restrictive baseline); no change in the measured health-outcome and malpractice proxies, specific to that setting
laboratory_counterpart: error under the status quo and under CF1 (no sign-off penalty), buffer against core
verdict: consistent for the buffer in direction; prices not modelled; the core is an untested prediction
construct: DIFFERENT: market prices and measured health outcomes in one service against synthetic packet error rates
unit_contrast: source: US states, restrictive versus permissive; laboratory: SQ against CF1 by ring
failure_criterion: buffer error rises materially when the sign-off penalty is removed

regularity: Entry standardization: new licensing standardizes entry and raises participation without a net wage benefit
source: Redbird (2017), American Sociological Review 82(3): licensing as entry standardization
laboratory_counterpart: incumbent stock at period 16 relative to period 1, licensed against unlicensed (mandatory disclosure)
verdict: not tested: the laboratory has no entry-standardization mechanism
note: post-shock stock growth in different occupations is not the licensing-employment effect; headcount here follows demand for signatures
construct: DIFFERENT: effect of adopting licensing on participation and wages against post-AI stock growth
unit_contrast: source: occupation-state panels over licensing adoption; laboratory: licensed vs unlicensed synthetic tasks after the tool
failure_criterion: requires an entry-standardization mechanism; none is modelled

regularity: Supply restriction: licensing raises wages and hours and reduces employment
source: Kleiner and Soltas (2023), Review of Economic Studies 90(5): occupations licensed differently across US states
laboratory_counterpart: incumbent stock at period 16 relative to period 1, licensed against unlicensed (mandatory disclosure)
verdict: not tested: the laboratory has no entry barrier or occupational wage
note: Redbird's entry-standardization and Kleiner-Soltas's supply-restriction findings concern different mechanisms, samples and outcomes and are not graded as one directional target
construct: DIFFERENT: cross-state licensing effect on wages, hours and employment against post-AI stock growth
unit_contrast: source: occupations licensed in some states only; laboratory: synthetic tasks
failure_criterion: requires a supply-restriction mechanism; none is modelled

regularity: No closure mechanism protects occupational pay against AI exposure
source: the programme (s605): bounded nulls for union, licensing, certification, credentials, associations
laboratory_counterpart: implied change in the log wage bill, licensed against unlicensed occupations
verdict: not comparable: the laboratory's unit-cost measure leans toward protection
note: the measures differ: a task's unit cost against an occupation's median wage
construct: DIFFERENT: occupational median wage against unit task cost
unit_contrast: source: occupations by closure type; laboratory: licensed vs unlicensed synthetic occupations
failure_criterion: requires an occupational wage; none is modelled

regularity: When technology takes the routine share of the work, trainees lose the practice that made them experts
source: Beane (2019) on surgical residents; Anthony (2021) on junior bankers
laboratory_counterpart: periods to eligibility at period 16 against the reference 8 (mandatory disclosure)
construct: related: qualitative accounts of lost practice against simulated periods to eligibility
unit_contrast: source: ethnographies of single settings; laboratory: synthetic cohorts
failure_criterion: periods to eligibility at or below the reference 8

regularity: A jurisdictional disturbance reaches the adjacent, less protected occupation first
source: Abbott (1988) on vacancy and bumping chains; the programme's lawyer/paralegal postings test (null so far)
laboratory_counterpart: subordinate and incumbent hours at the third compiler generation relative to the pre-tool division of labour
verdict: consistent with Abbott's account; not observed in the programme's postings data
note: the programme finds no break in the lawyer/paralegal ratio after guidance
evidence_class: AI-era consistency; empirical test so far null
construct: related: hours by occupation against postings ratios
unit_contrast: source: lawyer/paralegal postings; laboratory: bumping chains by ring
failure_criterion: incumbent hours fall before subordinate hours

regularity: Professions' own bodies subordinate AI rather than exclude it; exclusion comes from legislatures where harm is visible
source: the programme's census: own bodies 80 subordination rows, 9 exclusions; 13 of 15 binding exclusions are statutes
laboratory_counterpart: share of tasks gated under a regulator that sees only visible error, period 1 against 16
verdict: consistent in direction by the specified rule
evidence_class: AI-era consistency (follows from the specified regulator rule)
construct: DIFFERENT: rule-making bodies' choices against a regulator that gates on visible error
unit_contrast: source: rule rows by body type; laboratory: share of tasks gated by period
failure_criterion: gate share falls as visible error rises

regularity: Early-career workers in exposed occupations lose employment first
source: Brynjolfsson, Chandar, and Chen (2025): a 13 to 16% relative decline for ages 22 to 25
laboratory_counterpart: junior demand at period 16 relative to period 1 (mandatory disclosure), under the reference assumption that juniors operate the program and under the switch in which the program replaces junior hours
value: reference: licensed 173, unlicensed 150; program replaces juniors: licensed 69, unlicensed 75 (index, period 1 = 100)
verdict: junior DEMAND falls under the replacement switch and rises under the operator assumption; employment is not tested
note: demand is not headcount: the scenarios initialise stocks after the tool is present and normalise each to its own period 1, so neither is a causal effect relative to a common pre-AI population; stocks, hires, promotions and exits are reported separately in Table 9
construct: DIFFERENT: payroll employment by age against modelled junior labour demand
unit_contrast: source: payroll records, ages 22-25; laboratory: junior hours demanded per period
failure_criterion: not a test; one assignment decides the sign of demand

regularity: Statutory closure sits where errors harm third parties, in health, law, engineering and accounting
source: the public-interest account of licensing; the reference gate set (8 of 18 occupations)
laboratory_counterpart: best agreement of any pre-tool closure game (rent-seeking, visible-error or harm-weighted regulator) with the coded statutory gate set
how_it_arises: emergent (closure game on the pre-tool battle)
note: the failure has several candidate explanations (target coding, subordinate error prior, client cost rule, lobbying demand and cost, error visibility, task aggregation); it does not identify third-party harm as the missing theory; the externalised-liability variant is Table 15c
evidence_class: pre-AI institutional allocation (the one direct pre-tool test)
construct: related: a profession-level hand coding of sign-off (benchmark coding, not statute) against modelled gates
unit_contrast: source: 18 occupations, 8 coded gated; laboratory: closure game per occupation

regularity: After the AI shock, demand for statutory sign-off rises across occupations
source: the programme: licensing language in state AI bills rose from 3 mentions (2019 to 2022) to 52 (2025)
laboratory_counterpart: the gate's value to the profession in the AI era, every occupation; and visible harm without the gate
value: gain 11 to 15% of the wage per case in all 18 occupations; a captured regulator would gate 18 of 18
note: the visible harm that would justify the gate has vanished (Table 15)
construct: DIFFERENT: mentions of licensing in bills against modelled gate value
unit_contrast: source: state AI bills by year; laboratory: occupations
failure_criterion: gate value falls after the shock
